claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed jointly by ballistic atomic mixing and selective grain-boundary segregation of slowly diffusing elements.
Irradiation- or annealing-induced ballistic mixing suppresses local compositional fluctuations and eliminates incipient phase segregation.
Slowly diffusing elements such as Hf selectively segregate to grain boundaries.
Segregation of slowly diffusing elements strengthens grain boundaries and promotes defect recombination.
The two proposed effects maintain a refined, defect-tolerant, chemically homogenized microstructure.
The proposed initial state is a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a near-random elemental distribution.
Irradiation-driven mixing or high-temperature atomic mobility homogenizes the chemical distribution and counteracts thermally driven segregation.
Grain-boundary enrichment increases vacancy-interstitial recombination rates and thereby minimizes defect clustering.
The proposed dual mechanism suppresses precipitation that could destabilize the structure.
At approximately 1073-1173 K, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a refined grain size relative to conventional or less compositionally complex alloys.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit limited or suppressed precipitation under the proposed conditions.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit enhanced defect recombination under high-temperature conditions.
TEM will reveal fewer dislocation loops in the high-entropy nanoalloy than in the baseline alloy.
Stable grain boundaries will display characteristic elemental enrichment.
Conventional tungsten-based alloys or lower-complexity HEAs lacking the proposed mechanism tend to undergo more precipitation, grain coarsening, or defect-cluster formation.
The prediction applies to high-entropy nanoalloys with grain sizes below approximately 100 nm.
The prediction applies near, but not above, the alloy's threshold for significant diffusion or melting and may fail far above 1173 K.
The behavior may differ in coarse-grained bulk alloys.
Composition or processing changes can alter the order-disorder transition temperature and thereby change the proposed interplay.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits thermal annealing without irradiation, while the hypothesis requires ballistic mixing as one half of the dual mechanism. The mechanism later distinguishes irradiation-driven ballistic mixing from ordinary high-temperature atomic mobility, so annealing alone cannot directly instantiate the stated ballistic component.

The mechanism relies on sufficient high-temperature mobility for homogenization and grain-boundary segregation, whereas the boundary states that the prediction applies below the threshold for significant atomic diffusion. The required mobility regime is therefore not consistently defined.
